title: 452. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Angular Frequency and Period Relations
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the angular frequency of a periodic motion from its period.
questions.question: A periodic motion has period \(T=2\text{ s}\). What is its angular frequency \(\omega\)?
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is \(\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=\frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\text{ rad/s}\). Multiplying \(2\pi\) by the period instead of dividing gives \(4\pi\), which is incorrect.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the period of a periodic motion from its frequency.
questions.question: A signal has frequency \(f=5\text{ Hz}\). What is its period \(T\)?
questions.explanation: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency: \(T=\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2\text{ s}\). A frequency of \(5\text{ Hz}\) means \(5\) cycles each second, so one cycle lasts one fifth of a second, not \(5\) seconds.
questions.hint: Frequency counts cycles per second; the period is the time for one cycle.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a frequency in hertz to an angular frequency.
questions.question: A signal has frequency \(f=50\text{ Hz}\). What is its angular frequency \(\omega\)?
questions.explanation: Each cycle corresponds to \(2\pi\) radians, so \(\omega=2\pi f=2\pi\cdot 50=100\pi\text{ rad/s}\approx 314\text{ rad/s}\). Using \(\pi\) radians per cycle gives \(50\pi\), which is half the correct value.
questions.hint: One full cycle corresponds to \(2\pi\) radians.

questions.learningObjective: Convert an angular frequency to a frequency in hertz.
questions.question: A rotation has angular frequency \(\omega=8\pi\text{ rad/s}\). What is its frequency \(f\)?
questions.explanation: From \(\omega=2\pi f\), \(f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{8\pi}{2\pi}=4\text{ Hz}\). The number \(\frac{1}{4}\) is the period in seconds, \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=0.25\text{ s}\), not the frequency.

questions.learningObjective: Read the angular frequency from a rule and compute the period.
questions.question: A displacement is given by \(y=3\sin(6t)\), with \(t\) in seconds. What is the period of the motion?
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is the coefficient of \(t\), \(\omega=6\text{ rad/s}\). The period is \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3}\text{ s}\approx 1.05\text{ s}\). The number \(\frac{3}{\pi}\) is the frequency \(\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\) in hertz, the reciprocal of the period.
questions.hint: The coefficient of \(t\) is \(\omega\); then use \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\).

questions.learningObjective: Read the angular frequency from a rule and compute the frequency.
questions.question: A voltage is given by \(v=\cos(120\pi t)\), with \(t\) in seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is \(\omega=120\pi\text{ rad/s}\). The frequency is \(f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{120\pi}{2\pi}=60\text{ Hz}\). Dividing by \(\pi\) instead of \(2\pi\) gives \(120\), which is incorrect.

questions.concept: Angular speed from revolutions per minute
questions.learningObjective: Convert a rotation rate in revolutions per minute to radians per second.
questions.question: A wheel turns at \(300\) revolutions per minute. What is its angular speed in radians per second?
questions.explanation: Each revolution is \(2\pi\) radians, and one minute is \(60\) seconds: \(\omega=\frac{300\cdot 2\pi}{60}=10\pi\text{ rad/s}\). The value \(600\pi\) is the number of radians per minute, without the division by \(60\).
questions.hint: Convert revolutions to radians and minutes to seconds.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how the period changes when the frequency changes.
questions.question: The frequency of an oscillation is doubled. What happens to its period?
questions.explanation: The period is \(T=\frac{1}{f}\). Replacing \(f\) by \(2f\) gives \(\frac{1}{2f}=\frac{T}{2}\). More cycles per second means each cycle takes less time, so the period is halved.
questions.hint: The period and the frequency are reciprocals of each other.

questions.concept: Period from a small angular frequency
questions.learningObjective: Compute a period when the angular frequency is less than one radian per second.
questions.question: An oscillation has angular frequency \(\omega=0.5\text{ rad/s}\). What is its period?
questions.explanation: The period is \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi}{0.5}=4\pi\text{ s}\approx 12.6\text{ s}\). Multiplying \(2\pi\) by \(0.5\) instead of dividing gives \(\pi\text{ s}\), which is incorrect; a small angular frequency must give a long period.
questions.hint: Dividing by \(0.5\) is the same as multiplying by \(2\).

questions.learningObjective: Compare the periods of two sinusoids from their angular frequencies.
questions.question: Two signals are \(y_1=\sin(4\pi t)\) and \(y_2=\sin(6\pi t)\), with \(t\) in seconds. What is the ratio \(T_1:T_2\) of their periods?
questions.explanation: The periods are \(T_1=\frac{2\pi}{4\pi}=\frac{1}{2}\text{ s}\) and \(T_2=\frac{2\pi}{6\pi}=\frac{1}{3}\text{ s}\). The ratio is \(\frac{1}{2}:\frac{1}{3}=3:2\). The ratio \(2:3\) is the ratio of the angular frequencies; periods are inversely proportional to angular frequencies.
questions.hint: Compute each period with \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), then form the ratio.
